memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'Six days you shall labour, but on the seventh day you shall rest; even during the ploughing season and harvest you must rest.'" - Exod 34:21 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Look at that last clause. Even during ploughing and harvest.

Those were the two busiest, most financially critical weeks of an agricultural year. Miss the window and you lose the crop. And God says: rest anyway.

This is a command about trust before it is a command about scheduling. Anyone can rest when there is nothing urgent. Resting when everything feels urgent is an act of faith — a declaration that the harvest depends on God, not on my ability to work without stopping.

We live in a culture that treats exhaustion as evidence of importance. "I'm so busy" has become a way of saying "I matter." God's rhythm cuts straight through that. He built rest into creation itself before sin ever entered the world (Gen 2:2-3).

Christians hold different convictions about how the Sabbath applies today, and Scripture leaves room for that (Rom 14:5-6; Col 2:16-17). We will not settle that here. But the principle underneath is not optional: we are creatures, not machines, and God has designed us to stop.

Jesus said the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). It is a gift, not a burden. And He offers a deeper rest still — rest for the soul (Matt 11:29).

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do you rest, or only collapse when you can no longer continue?
2. What does your inability to stop reveal about what you trust?
3. What would a genuinely restful day look like for you?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, I confess I trust my own effort more than I should. Teach me to stop, and to rest in You. Amen.
